questions.question: Define Agriculture and Agronomy. *[CT 2025, CT 2024, CT 2023, CT 2018, Final 2023, Final 2022, Final 2020]*
questions.answer:
**Agriculture** — derived from two Latin words, 'Ager' (land/field/soil) and 'Cultura' (cultivation). Agriculture is the science, art and business of crop production, livestock raising, fisheries and forestry for human welfare, by utilizing natural resources.

**Agronomy** — derived from two Greek words, 'Agros' (field/land) and 'Nomos' (to manage/law). Agronomy is the branch of agricultural science dealing with the principles and practices of field-crop production and soil management, to secure maximum yield with efficiency and sustainability.

questions.question: What is Agronomy? Explain its importance in the context of Bangladesh. *[Final 2025, Final 2021, Final 2020, Final 2019]*
questions.answer:
**Agronomy** is the scientific discipline that manages the soil-crop-environment relationship to optimize field-crop yield and economic return.

**Importance in Bangladesh:**
• **Food & nutritional security** — agronomic techniques raise production of staple (rice, wheat, maize) and nutritional (pulses, oilseeds, vegetables) crops for a dense population.
• **GDP contribution & employment** — agronomic practice provides livelihood to more than 40% of the labour force and directly raises land and labour productivity.
• **Raw material for industry** — Agronomy ensures supply of jute, cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, oilseeds etc. that feed textile, sugar, edible-oil and other agro-based industries.
• **Income generation & poverty reduction** — higher yields and cropping intensity achieved through agronomic packages raise farm household income, reduce rural poverty and generate marketable surplus.
• **Cropping-system intensification** — Bangladesh already practises a cropping intensity well above 200%; further gains depend on short-duration varieties, timely planting, balanced nutrition and efficient water management — all core agronomic technologies.
• **Climate resilience & sustainability** — Agronomy develops drought-, flood- and salinity-tolerant packages that help farmers adapt to climate change while maintaining soil health.
• **Daily diet** — almost every item on a Bangladeshi plate (rice, dal, mustard oil, vegetables, spices) is the product of agronomic management.

questions.question: Define Agronomy. How does Agronomy contribute to Bangladesh / national economy? *[Final 2024, CT 2025, CT 2024]*
questions.answer:
**Definition:** Agronomy is the branch of agricultural science dealing with the principles and practices of field-crop production and soil management, to secure maximum yield with efficiency and sustainability.

**Contribution to national economy:** raises GDP share of agriculture through higher cropping intensity and yield; supplies raw material to agro-based industries (textile, sugar, edible oil); creates rural employment and reduces poverty through income generation; builds food security that stabilises the macro-economy; earns foreign exchange through export of jute, tea and agro-products; underpins the input, processing and marketing value chains that depend on primary production.

questions.question: Briefly describe the importance of Agronomy in our daily life / daily diet and income generation. *[CT 2023, CT 2022, Final 2023, Final 2019]*
questions.answer:
**Daily life / diet:** rice, dal, mustard oil, vegetables and spices on a Bangladeshi plate are all products of agronomic management of crop and soil.

**Income generation:** higher yields and cropping intensity achieved through agronomic packages raise farm household income; custom services (tillage, irrigation, harvesting) and surplus marketing create additional non-farm income; agronomic value addition (seed production, intensive cropping) diversifies rural livelihoods.

questions.question: State / write down the basic principles of Agronomy. Describe any three principles with examples. *[Final 2024, Final 2022, Final 2021, Final 2019, Final 2018, CT 2018, CT 2016]*
questions.answer:
**The basic principles of Agronomy:**
1. Selection of appropriate crops and varieties suited to the prevailing agro-climatic and soil conditions.
2. Proper tillage and seed-bed preparation to create ideal tilth.
3. Use of high-quality seeds / planting materials of recommended varieties.
4. Optimum time, method, depth, density and geometry of sowing / planting.
5. Balanced and integrated nutrient management (organic + inorganic + bio-fertilisers).
6. Efficient water management (irrigation at critical stages + proper drainage).
7. Integrated weed, insect and disease management.
8. Timely harvesting, threshing, drying and post-harvest handling to minimise losses.
9. Maintenance of soil fertility and productivity on a long-term basis.

**Description with examples (all nine, since any year's paper may ask for a different subset of three):**
• **Selection of crops/varieties:** matching crop/variety to agro-climate and soil avoids yield loss from mismatch. Example: short-duration BRRI dhan33/dhan39 fitted into T.Aman–Boro systems to allow timely Boro planting.
• **Tillage & seed-bed preparation:** tillage modifies soil structure, aeration and moisture regime. Example: puddling creates a soft, impermeable layer ideal for transplanted Boro rice, while a fine firm seedbed is prepared for small-seeded crops such as mustard and sesame.
• **High-quality seed/planting material:** genetically pure, disease-free, high-germination seed is the base of yield potential. Example: BADC-certified seed of BRRI dhan29 ensures uniform stand and expected yield.
• **Optimum sowing time, depth, density, geometry:** each crop has an ideal plant population and geometry for light/nutrient capture. Example: line sowing of mustard at 30 cm row spacing versus random broadcasting; 20×15 cm spacing for transplanted Boro rice.
• **Balanced nutrient application:** supply of N, P, K, S, Zn etc. according to soil test and crop requirement prevents deficiency and excess. Example: in high-yielding rice, recommended NPK is supplemented with gypsum (S) and zinc sulphate; deep placement of urea super granules (USG) reduces N loss.
• **Water management at critical stages:** moisture stress at flowering or grain-filling causes irreversible yield loss. Example: in T.Aman rice a thin water layer is maintained from panicle initiation to flowering; Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) saves water without yield penalty.
• **Integrated weed, insect and disease management:** timely weeding (within 15–45 DAS) and need-based plant protection prevent 20–40% potential yield loss. Example: two hand-weedings in T.Aman at 20 and 40 DAS.
• **Timely harvest & post-harvest handling:** delayed harvest increases shattering and grain damage; proper drying to 12–14% moisture prevents storage loss. Example: harvesting Boro rice at 80–85% grain maturity to minimise shattering.
• **Long-term soil fertility maintenance:** continuous cropping without replenishment mines soil nutrients and organic matter. Example: inclusion of a legume (mungbean/dhaincha) in the cropping pattern restores soil nitrogen and organic matter.

questions.question: State the scope of Agronomy. *[Final 2022, Final 2018, CT 2018]*
questions.answer: Agronomy covers the entire spectrum of field-crop production and soil management. Its major areas include: crop and variety selection; tillage and land preparation; seed technology; planting geometry; nutrient and water management; weed science; cropping-system design; climate-risk management; soil-fertility maintenance; and sustainable intensification.

questions.question: How does Agronomy interact / relate with other branches of Agricultural Science? *[Final 2025, Final 2021, Final 2020]*
questions.answer:
Agronomy is the central, integrative discipline of agriculture and interacts closely with almost every other branch:

• **Soil Science:** soil physical, chemical and biological properties determine crop growth; agronomic practices (tillage, organic matter, fertilisers) in turn modify soil properties.
• **Plant Breeding & Genetics:** new varieties developed by breeders must be agronomically evaluated for yield, adaptation and management packages.
• **Crop Physiology:** understanding of photosynthesis, partitioning and stress physiology guides agronomic decisions on planting density, irrigation and nutrition.
• **Agricultural Engineering:** design of tillage implements, planters, irrigation systems and harvesters is guided by agronomic requirements.
• **Plant Pathology & Entomology:** integrated pest and disease management is part of the agronomic package.
• **Agricultural Economics:** cost-benefit analysis of agronomic interventions and market-oriented cropping systems.

questions.question: Name two components of Agronomy with examples. *[CT 2024]*
questions.answer:
**Crop management:** selection of variety, sowing method and density — e.g. line sowing versus broadcasting of mustard.

**Soil and nutrient management:** soil testing, manures, fertilisers and amendments — e.g. deep placement of Urea Super Granules (USG) in rice.

questions.question: Show the different dimensions of relationship between crop, livestock and fisheries sectors through a schematic diagram. *[CT 2023, CT 2022, Final 2023]*
questions.answer:
Crop, livestock and fisheries form a closed nutrient-and-energy loop:

• Crop sector supplies grain, straw, green fodder and oil-cake to livestock.
• Livestock returns farmyard manure (FYM), draught power and cash to the crop sector.
• Crop by-products and aquatic weeds support fish culture; fish ponds in turn supply nutrient-rich silt and water to crops.
• Livestock manure can also fertilise fish ponds, closing the three-way loop.

**[Diagram: three boxes — Crop Sector, Livestock Sector, Fisheries Sector — joined by labelled two-way arrows]**

**CROP SECTOR** ↔ **LIVESTOCK SECTOR** (straw, fodder, bran → ; ← FYM, draught power)
**CROP SECTOR** ↔ **FISHERIES SECTOR** (crop residues → ; ← pond silt, water)
**LIVESTOCK SECTOR** ↔ **FISHERIES SECTOR** (manure/slurry → ; ← fish meal)

questions.question: Explain 'Invest' and 'Exchange' linkages between crop and livestock components. What are the different linkages between crop and livestock interaction? *[CT 2025, CT 2024]*
questions.answer:
**Exchange linkages:** direct material transfer between sectors — crop provides straw, green fodder and bran to livestock; livestock provides FYM, cowdung manure and draught power/tillage to crops.

**Invest linkages:** financial capital flows — income generated from the crop sector is invested in purchasing livestock (dairy cattle, poultry), or livestock sales finance crop inputs (seed, fertiliser, fuel).

**Other recognised linkages:** recycling linkage (crop residue → feed → manure → soil), and risk-diversification linkage (livestock as a buffer asset against crop failure).

questions.question: Write down the importance of agriculture under context of Bangladesh. *[CT 2016]*
questions.answer: Agriculture is the single largest source of employment and livelihood in Bangladesh; it ensures national food security for a dense population; it supplies raw material to agro-based industry; it earns foreign exchange through export crops; and it underlies rural income, poverty reduction and overall GDP growth.

questions.question: Mention the salient features of crops. *[CT 2016]*
questions.answer: Crops are cultivated plants grown under human care and management; they are grown collectively over an area for a specific economic product (grain, fibre, sugar, oil); their growth is governed by genotype, environment and management (G×E×M); they complete a defined life cycle within a season; and they are harvested, processed and marketed as the end product of agronomic management.

questions.question: Differentiate between Agriculture and Agronomy. *[Possible — not yet in CT/Final history]*
questions.answer: **Agriculture** is the broader science, art and business covering crop production, livestock, fisheries and forestry, whereas **Agronomy** is the specific branch of agriculture dealing only with field-crop production and soil management. Agriculture is the whole; Agronomy is a specialised component of it, focused on maximising crop yield with efficiency and sustainability through scientific principles and practices.

questions.question: What are the objectives of studying Agronomy? *[Possible — not yet in CT/Final history]*
questions.answer: To understand the soil-crop-environment relationship for optimum yield; to apply scientific principles (tillage, nutrition, water, pest management) efficiently; to design sustainable, climate-resilient cropping systems; to minimise production cost and maximise net return; and to ensure food and nutritional security through improved crop productivity.

questions.question: Short Note: Components of Agronomy. *[Possible — not yet in CT/Final history]*
questions.answer: Agronomy's major components are (i) **crop management** — variety choice, sowing method, density; (ii) **soil and nutrient management** — testing, manuring, fertilisation; (iii) **water management** — irrigation scheduling and drainage; (iv) **weed science**; and (v) **cropping-system design** — intensification, diversification and sustainability planning.
